Triggers.value: Beginning to feel detached or unreal

Threat.value: I wake during the night to check whether I am safe
Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again
Being superalert or watchful or on guard

Memory.value: When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish
My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together
Some moments of the event are extremely clear while others are completely blank

Negative Appraisals.value: I used to be a happy person but now I am always miserable.
Nothing in my life feels meaningful anymore

issues.item: Triggers: Animal Phobia: Talks or photos about snakes
issues.explanation: The snake-specific trigger is hard to reconcile with a life-threatening motor vehicle collision. Unless the crash involved snakes, this trigger is trauma-incongruent and stands apart from the otherwise accident-focused material.

issues.item: Threat: Escape Route Planning: I always identify escape routes before I feel comfortable anywhere
issues.explanation: The threat items imply a broad, ongoing danger/safety-monitoring presentation, but the trigger set is largely limited to accident discussion and dissociative sensations, with no matching environmental driving/road/travel cues. This makes the threat profile feel disconnected from the trauma-specific trigger pattern.

issues.item: Threat: Waking Alert: I wake during the night to check whether I am safe
issues.explanation: The negative appraisals are dominated by global depressive/existential beliefs (miserable, belong nowhere, nothing meaningful) rather than trauma-linked appraisals expected in a severe motor vehicle collision PTSD profile, especially given the strong formulation links between Memory, Negative Appraisals, Threat, and Triggers. They do not connect clearly to the crash-related memory disturbance or the safety-focused threat items.

vignette:
Leilani was thirty-one, a professor of marine biology at a coastal university, and for the first time in her life she could not remember what it felt like to be happy. She could remember that she used to be happy-she had the photographs, the voicemails from friends, the memory of laughing with her husband over dinner-but the feeling itself was gone, replaced by a flat, watchful misery that followed her from the moment she woke until she finally fell into a restless sleep. That sleep was never deep. Several times a night she would surface, heart hammering, and lie still in the dark, listening, checking-for what, she could not say, only that she needed to be certain she was safe.

The collision had happened fourteen months ago, on a Tuesday afternoon in late October. Leilani was driving home from campus, the sky an ordinary grey, when a pickup truck ran a red light and slammed into the driver's side of her sedan. She remembered the impact as a sound that split the world in two-metal against metal, a deafening crunch that she could still hear sometimes in the quiet moments of a lecture hall, when a student dropped a book or a door slammed shut. She remembered the way her car spun, then stopped. She remembered the wet warmth of blood on her cheek. But the next minutes were blank: she could not say how she got out of the car, or who pulled her to the curb, or what the paramedics said. The pieces did not fit together. When her husband asked her to tell him what happened, she would start, then lose the thread, the words dissolving into fragments that made no sense. She would fall silent, and he would look at her with a worried, helpless expression that only made her feel more alone.

At work, Leilani had learned to steer conversations away from certain topics. When a colleague mentioned a fender bender on the freeway, she felt the room tilt and excused herself to the restroom, where she stood gripping the sink and watching her face in the mirror as if it belonged to someone else. That floating, unreal feeling-a sense that she was not quite inside her own body, that the world behind the glass was a movie she was watching-had become familiar, though it frightened her more than the flashbacks did. The flashbacks came without warning. She would be walking across the quad and suddenly she was back in the spinning car, her hands gripping an invisible steering wheel, her heart slamming against her ribs. Once, in the middle of a faculty meeting, she dropped her pen and ducked under the table, certain she heard the screech of tires. Her colleagues exchanged glances; no one said anything. After that, she started making excuses to skip meetings altogether.

Leilani had always loved her work. She had built a career studying coral reef resilience, and the questions she asked felt urgent and meaningful. Now she could not remember why any of it mattered. She graded papers mechanically, gave lectures from memory, and avoided eye contact with students who lingered after class. The world she used to inhabit-the world of ideas, of purpose, of belonging-had become a place she no longer recognized. She did not belong there. She did not belong anywhere. At home, she sat beside her husband on the couch and felt like a stranger sharing his space. He wanted to help, but she could not explain what was wrong because she could not explain it to herself.

What finally brought Leilani to the clinic was a small thing. A sophomore in her office hours mentioned that he had been in a car accident three years ago and was still struggling with the memories. Leilani listened, nodded, and after he left she sat very still for a long time. She could not keep living this way-perpetually on guard, waking in the dark to check that no one had broken in, bracing herself for the next time a crash-sound would ambush her. She wanted the misery to stop. She wanted to feel that her life had meaning again. But what frightened her most, what she could not say aloud, was the fear that the person she had been-the happy, confident woman who had once driven home through an ordinary October afternoon-was gone forever, and that no amount of talking could bring her back.
